title: A Century-Old Medical Mystery: The Enigma of the 'Sleeping Sickness'
summary: In the shadow of the 1918 Spanish Flu, a far stranger pandemic unfolded. Encephalitis lethargica (EL), nicknamed "sleeping sickness," struck without warning, plunging victims into profound sleep that could last weeks or months—or, in some cases, whipping them into a frenzy of manic activity. Austrian physician Constantin von Economo first documented it in 1917, describing a "delirious somnolence" from which patients could be roused but often remained confused. The disease killed roughly 500,000 people between 1917 and 1930 and left many survivors with permanent Parkinsonism, personality changes, or psychosis. Children were especially vulnerable to lasting damage. The coincidence of EL with the Spanish Flu led many to suspect a link. After all, a similar neurological syndrome had accompanied an 1889 influenza epidemic. But EL persisted a decade after the flu vanished, and modern analysis of historic brain samples has never found influenza virus traces. In 2012, researchers proposed an enterovirus—the family that includes polio—as the culprit, since some strains cause muscle weakness. Others favor an autoimmune theory, though that struggles to explain the pandemic's wide spread. The last known survivor, Philip Leather, died in 2002 after decades immobile in a mental hospital. Today, EL is vanishingly rare: only 80 cases have been reported in the past 85 years. Yet the lack of a definitive cause leaves an unsettling question: could this forgotten plague reawaken? For now, it remains one of medicine's most haunting unsolved riddles.
why_it_matters: Encephalitis lethargica is a chilling reminder that not every global health threat comes from a known enemy—future diseases could just as easily appear without warning, and understanding past mysteries is key to being prepared.

background_read: Encephalitis lethargica emerged during the final years of World War I, killing thousands in war-torn Europe already devastated by poverty and hunger.

The Spanish Flu, which erupted in 1918, killed at least 50 million people globally—five percent of the world’s population at the time—and its overlap with sleeping sickness led doctors to suspect a connection, though never proven.

Constantin von Economo (an Austrian neurologist) not only described the disease but also traced a pattern: many victims first experienced a flu-like illness, then fell into a long sleep or became bizarrely hyperactive, a clue that a virus might trigger it.

Polio, another member of the enterovirus family, paralyzed hundreds of thousands of children each year before vaccines emerged in the 1950s, showing how nerve-damaging viruses can sweep through populations and leave lifelong scars.

Today, extremely rare neurodegenerative outbreaks are monitored by global health bodies like the WHO because history shows that a small cluster can balloon into a worldwide tragedy if a pathogen finds the right conditions to spread.

perspectives.description: Studying EL advanced neuroscience and post-infectious disease research, leading to better understanding of Parkinsonism and brain inflammation. The 2012 enterovirus clue opens doors for research that might prevent future neurological pandemics.

Because we still don't know exactly what caused the original outbreak, public health systems could miss early warning signs. A new strain could spread before anyone identifies it, especially in regions with weak healthcare surveillance.

History shows that some severe neurological syndromes appear during or just after large respiratory pandemics—a link seen in 1889, 1918, and to a lesser extent in COVID-19. The mechanism might involve the immune system overreacting rather than a single virus directly attacking the brain.

Scientists call for international brain-sample banks and faster viral genomic surveillance so that if a cluster of similar cases appears anywhere, teams can rapidly compare data and potentially develop treatments before it becomes a crisis.
